title: He was forgiven everything…
paragraphs:
He was forgiven everything…
but he couldn’t forgive a little.
Because this is where the story turns—and where it exposes us.
Or nodded your head and thought, “Yeah, that’s terrible.”

But what if…
you are not the observer in the story?
What if you are the servant?

And what if the hands around that man’s throat…
feel strangely familiar?
He told stories that corner you.
Stories that force you to see yourself when you’d rather stay hidden.
In Matthew 18:21–35, a man is drowning in debt.

Some scholars interpret the amount Jesus used—ten thousand talents—as intentionally absurd, a number meant to communicate impossibility. In modern terms, it would be like owing billions. Lifetimes of labor couldn’t fix it.
So he does the only thing left.
“Have patience with me, and I will pay you everything.” (Matthew 18:26)
That’s what makes what happens next so shocking.
“So out of pity for him, the master of that servant released him and forgave him the debt.” (Matthew 18:27)
Imagine the weight lifting off his chest.
The suffocation of fear replaced with breath.
The crushing shame replaced with mercy.
But something didn’t change inside him.
Because the story doesn’t end there.
Same man who just received impossible mercy.
Same man who was just rescued from total ruin.
And finds someone who owes him.
“And he seized him and began to choke him, saying, ‘Pay what you owe.’” (Matthew 18:28)
That shift lives in us too.
This is not just about ancient coins and servants.
This is about that person you still haven’t forgiven.
That wound that replays in your mind at 2AM.
That memory that tightens your chest.
But here’s the question this parable forces on us:
Because the danger is not just unforgiveness.

When you forget the size of your forgiven debt…
you exaggerate the debts of others.

When you minimize your sin…
you maximize their offense.
You become the man in the story.
Look again at what happens next.
The fellow servant falls to his knees.
“Have patience with me, and I will pay you.” (Matthew 18:29)
“He went and put him in prison until he should pay the debt.” (Matthew 18:30)
It imprisons others in your heart.
You rehearse conversations that never happened.
You build a courtroom in your mind where you are always the judge…
But here’s the truth we don’t like:

Unforgiveness feels like control…
but it is actually bondage.
When the master hears what happened, everything changes.
“Should not you have had mercy on your fellow servant, as I had mercy on you?” (Matthew 18:33)
Forgiveness is not optional for the forgiven.
It is proof that grace actually reached your heart.
Forgiveness is not pretending nothing happened.
It is not saying abuse is okay.
It is not removing boundaries or ignoring wisdom.
It is not instant emotional healing.

Releasing your right to be the final judge…
and placing the case in God’s hands.
“Beloved, never avenge yourselves, but leave it to the wrath of God…” (Romans 12:19)
You don’t have to carry that weight anymore.
Because this is not just about behavior.
We stood before God with a debt we could never pay.
“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.” (Romans 3:23)
And we had nothing to offer.
“But God shows his love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.” (Romans 5:8)
That means your debt—if you are in Christ—is gone.
So how can we stand at the cross…
See the Son of God bleeding for our forgiveness…
And then walk away refusing to forgive someone else?
Because unforgiveness is not just a relational issue.
“For if you forgive others their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you, but if you do not forgive others… neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.” (Matthew 6:14–15)
This is not saying we earn forgiveness.
It is saying forgiven hearts forgive.
If there is no evidence of mercy flowing out…
We must ask if mercy has truly been received.
So where does that leave you?
Whose offense have you rehearsed more than you’ve released?

“Lord, I don’t want to forgive.
But I want to want to forgive.
Help me.”
You are not asked to forgive in your own strength.
You are invited to forgive from His.
“The love of Christ controls us…” (2 Corinthians 5:14)
When His cross becomes real again…
So let me ask you one more time.

Are you holding someone by the throat…
while standing under the shadow of the cross?
If this is speaking to you…
And if this stirred something deep inside you…
